note: Species info for info pages. Sizes are typical ranges; weights are fun comparisons. Edit freely.

black-capped-chickadee.nest: Hole it digs in soft, rotting wood
facts: The more "dee"s in its call, the bigger the danger nearby.
Part of its brain grows each fall to help it remember where it hid food.
Carries up to 5 acorns at once in its throat and beak.
Helped oak forests spread north after the Ice Age by burying acorns.

american-crow.diet: Almost anything: insects, grain, eggs, scraps
american-crow.nest: Big stick nest high in a tree
facts: Young crows often stay with their parents for years and help raise siblings.
Gathers by the thousands in winter roosts.

northern-cardinal.nest: Cup of twigs in a dense shrub
facts: Females sing too, often from the nest.
Males fight their own reflection in windows in spring.
Hoards seeds one at a time, usually within 130 feet of a feeder.
A pointed gray crest it raises when excited.
Wedges nuts into bark and hacks them open, which is how it got its name.
Pairs stay together all year.

red-breasted-nuthatch.nest: Hole it digs in a dead tree
facts: Some winters it flies far south when pinecone crops fail.
Steals pitch from other birds' trees to coat its own door.

downy-woodpecker.nest: Hole it drills in a dead branch
facts: Males feed more on small branches, females on bigger ones.
Drums on trees in spring to say "this is my spot".

hairy-woodpecker.nest: Hole it drills in a live or dead tree
facts: Its sharp "peek!" is louder and higher than a Downy's.
Its tongue wraps around inside its skull.

pileated-woodpecker.nest: Big hole in a dead tree
facts: Its old holes become homes for ducks, owls and bats.
Rips off big strips of bark looking for ants.

american-goldfinch.nest: Tight cup woven so well it can hold water
facts: One of the few birds that eats almost only seeds.
Nests late in summer, when thistle down is ready for lining.
One was found with over 17,000 tiny seeds stored in its throat.
Parents feed their chicks "crop milk" they make themselves.
Copies car alarms, phones and other birds.
Huge flocks swirl together in shapes called murmurations.
People have kept pigeons for over 5,000 years.
Carried messages in both World Wars.

dark-eyed-junco.nest: Cup on the ground, under a log or bank
facts: Flashes white tail feathers when it flies off.
One of the most common birds in North America.
Eats more fruit in fall and winter, worms in spring and summer.
Can raise three families in one summer.

song-sparrow.nest: Cup on or near the ground
facts: Young males learn their songs from neighbors.
Pumps its tail up and down as it flies.

cedar-waxwing.nest: Loose cup in a tree fork
facts: Waxy red tips on its wings give it its name.
Flock-mates pass berries beak to beak down a branch.

bald-eagle.nest: Huge stick nest that can weigh a ton
facts: Nests can be 10 feet wide and are reused for decades.
Takes 5 years to get its white head.

red-tailed-hawk.nest: Stick nest high in a tree
facts: Often perches on highway light poles watching for mice.
Its rusty-red tail gives it away.

osprey.nest: Big stick nest on poles, towers and treetops
facts: Can close its nostrils when it dives.
Turns a fish head-first while flying to cut wind drag.
One of the few animals that eats skunks.
Its grip is strong enough to crush prey.

barred-owl.voice: "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"
facts: Has dark brown eyes, unlike most owls.
Pairs "duet" with wild hoots and cackles.
Males get whiter as they age.
One owl can eat over 1,600 lemmings a year.

red-winged-blackbird.nest: Cup tied to cattails or reeds
facts: One of the first birds back each spring.
A male may have several mates in his patch of cattails.

common-yellowthroat.nest: Bulky cup low in grass or shrubs
facts: Hides in thick, wet tangles; listen for it first.
Females don't have the black mask.

yellow-warbler.nest: Neat cup in a shrub fork
facts: Males have red streaks on their yellow chest.
Spends winter in Central and South America.
Sings hundreds of times an hour in early summer.
Flies to Mexico and Central America for winter.

red-eyed-vireo.nest: Hanging cup in a branch fork
red-eyed-vireo.voice: "Here I am. Where are you?" over and over
facts: Its red eyes are brown when it's young.
One of the most common forest birds in the East.
Its songs can last 10 minutes without repeating.
Hides a rusty patch under its tail.

ruby-throated-hummingbird.nest: Thimble-sized cup glued with spider silk
facts: Beats its wings about 50 times a second.
Can fly backwards.

tree-swallow.nest: Tree hole or nest box lined with feathers
facts: Eats bayberries in cold snaps, unlike most swallows.
Gathers in flocks of thousands before migrating.

great-blue-heron.nest: Stick nest in colonies high in trees
facts: Weighs only 5 to 6 pounds thanks to hollow bones.
Special neck bones let it strike like a spring.

double-crested-cormorant.nest: Stick nest in colonies on islands
facts: Can dive about 25 feet to chase fish.
The "double crest" is two tufts that only show in spring.

eastern-phoebe.nest: Mud and moss cup under porches and bridges
facts: Wags its tail constantly.
First bird ever banded in North America, by Audubon in 1804.

bobolink.nest: Cup on the ground in hayfields
facts: Males look like they're wearing a tuxedo on backwards.
Navigates partly by Earth's magnetic field.
Its eyes sit so far back it can see behind itself.
Bobs its body to make worms move underground.
Chicks run around within hours of hatching.
Nests on parking lots and gravel roofs.
Loves orange halves and grape jelly at feeders.
Named for Lord Baltimore, whose colors were orange and black.

scarlet-tanager.nest: Shallow cup high in an oak
facts: Males turn yellow-green after summer.
Winters in South America.
Chicks peck the red spot on a parent's bill to ask for food.
Takes 4 years to get adult gray-and-white plumage.
Bosses other gulls around at the beach.
Can swallow a whole duckling.
Swallows mussels whole and crushes the shells in its gizzard.
Mothers share babysitting in groups called crèches.

mallard.nest: Grass bowl on the ground near water
facts: Only female Mallards make the classic quack.
Ducklings can swim right after hatching.
Flashes purple-blue wing patches in flight.
Very wary; flushes at the first sign of people.
Its solid bones help it dive up to 200 feet.
Can barely walk on land, so nests right at the water.
Males wear down their brown feather tips to turn white in spring.
Nests farther north than almost any songbird.
Name means "buffalo-head" for its puffy head.
One of the smallest diving ducks.
Has different summer and winter outfits, changing feathers often.
Flies with fast, swinging wingbeats low over the sea.
Ducklings jump from tree holes 40 feet up on day one.
Males throw their heads back in courtship.
Has a faint purple sheen you can only see up close.
Winters farther north than any other shorebird on the East Coast.
Can store extra seeds in its throat to survive cold nights.
Yellow flashes hide in its wings and tail.

evening-grosbeak.nest: Loose cup high in a conifer
facts: Its huge bill cracks cherry pits.
Was once a winter feeder regular in Maine; now much rarer.
"Semipalmated" means its toes are half-webbed.
Doubles its weight in about two weeks before flying south.
Its black belly only shows in spring and summer.
Hunts by run, stop, peck.
